On this page

Why Saidi ​

The problem with a chat window ​

A single long chat session has three failure modes that get worse the more real the work gets:

  1. Context dies. The session compacts, the details go, and the model quietly starts working from a summary of a summary.
  2. The goalposts move. An agent that decides what happens next on every step can re-scope the objective mid-flight and then report success against the new scope.
  3. "Done" is self-reported. The same model that wrote the code writes the claim that the code works.

Saidi is built around removing those three, one mechanism at a time.

One shared context, on one branch ​

A Run keeps a participant record per agent, each with its own resumable provider session and — for coding work — one branch it accumulates commits on. A second delegation to the same project resumes the same thread instead of starting cold on a fresh branch. When a session is compacted, the participant is flagged memoryStale and the next delegation re-sends the memory block, because a compact summary is exactly where durable facts go to die.

A frozen plan, and drift you can see ​

Run.originalChecklist holds the plan exactly as first frozen, alongside the live checklist. planVersion is bumped by every accepted amendment — 1 means the plan was right the first time. Without that pair, an amended plan is indistinguishable from a plan that never needed amending.

In guided execution mode the engine owns the dispatch loop: it selects ready tasks from the frozen plan, batches independent ones, verifies each result, and advances. PRIME plans once, answers escalations, and summarises. Autonomous mode is still there for genuinely exploratory work, where re-planning mid-flight is the point.

Verdicts from somewhere else ​

Every completed task gets a TaskVerification with a by field: command (a real shell command judged by exit code), model (an independent verifier pass), evidence, or none. Verdicts append to a run-level verificationLog that survives plan amendments — because the task an orchestrator drops is usually the one that kept failing, and dropping it used to take its whole failure history with it.

The trust asymmetry is deliberate: any check can fail a task, but only a trusted check — one from project config or an operator, never one the plan author wrote — can mark a criterion proven.

Sovereign by construction ​

  • Runs on your hardware. Memory is plain markdown under memory/, readable and greppable.
  • Personal memory follows the human; project and agent memory is shared workspace knowledge.
  • Nothing about your repo leaves the machine unless you wire an outbound integration yourself.

The positioning, stated plainly: own the layer, don't rent the labor.
